---
title: "Synthesis and argument map"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-28"
---

Use one map per consequential paragraph, section claim or decision. Every cited source must still be opened and checked.

## Blank map

**Question this section answers:** [ ]
**Bounded claim:** [ ]
**Why the claim matters:** [ ]

| Role | What belongs here | Source and exact location |
|---|---|---|
| Supporting evidence | [direct evidence or reasoning] | [ ] |
| Qualifying evidence | [condition, uncertainty or subgroup] | [ ] |
| Contrary evidence | [credible challenge or alternative] | [ ] |
| Warrant | [why the evidence justifies the claim] | [ ] |
| Boundary | [where the claim should not be assumed] | [ ] |

**Alternative explanation:** [ ]
**Sentence that would overclaim:** [ ]
**Defensible paragraph sequence:** claim → comparison → warrant → boundary → consequence
**Remaining evidence needed:** [ ]

## Completed example

**Question:** What makes feedback usable during candidature?

**Bounded claim:** Feedback is more likely to be actionable when it identifies the goal, current performance and a feasible next step, but this does not guarantee improved doctoral outcomes.

| Role | Entry | Source location |
|---|---|---|
| Supporting evidence | broad feedback model distinguishes goal, performance and next steps | Hattie and Timperley, model section |
| Qualifying evidence | effects vary with information content and setting | Wisniewski and colleagues, results/discussion |
| Contrary evidence | none yet located for the exact mechanism | unresolved question logged |
| Warrant | specific information can be converted into an observable revision | writer's inference, labelled |
| Boundary | evidence base is broader education, not doctoral supervision alone | source scope |

**Sentence that would overclaim:** “Supervisor feedback following this model improves PhD completion.”

**Defensible consequence:** Use the model to structure a feedback request while seeking doctorate-specific evidence and tracking whether the resulting revision is actually possible.

## Scenario test

Your paragraph has six citations after one broad sentence. Map each source to the exact part it supports. Split the claim if the sources support different mechanisms or populations. Remove any citation that is merely topically related, and add an explicit boundary if the combined evidence is narrower than the sentence.
